Customers use the activity feed and its export as an audit trail. Support has these reports:

1. Filtering the feed by project hides status changes, comments, comment edits and comment deletions. They only show up in the unfiltered feed, or not at all.
2. When someone assigns an issue, the entry names the assignee as the person who did it rather than the person who assigned.
3. Several kinds of action never appear at all: issues being edited or archived, projects being edited or restored, comments being edited or deleted, members joining or being removed, and feature switches being toggled.
4. Entries are stamped with the time they were written rather than the time the action happened. A background job that catches up later files things under the wrong time, and a time-range filter then misses them.
5. An export never contains more than 100 entries, whatever the range. Exporting with "from" and "to" set to the same instant returns nothing, and an entry that happened exactly at the end of a range is missing from it.
6. The JSON export used to include each entry's details, for instance the old and new status of a status change. Those are now empty.

- Every action someone takes in a workspace appears in the activity log exactly once: creating, editing, archiving and restoring a project; creating, editing, assigning, changing the status of and archiving an issue; posting, editing and deleting a comment; inviting, joining, changing the role of and removing a member; changing the plan; toggling a feature switch; changing the workspace settings. Each entry names the person who did it. Entries about a project, an issue or a comment carry the project they belong to, so filtering the feed by project shows everything that happened inside that project, including comments, comment edits and deletions, status changes and assignments, and nothing from other projects.

- A time range includes both of its ends. A range whose start and end are the same instant returns the entries at that instant. A range that ends before it starts is refused.

tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem. You can access any file directly by using this tool.
Assume this tool is able to read all files on the machine. If the User provides a path to a file assume that path is valid. It is okay to read a file that does not exist; an error will be returned.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

### 1. Where activity entries are created

`record()` in `src/server/services/activity-service.ts:50-66` is the single low-level writer:

```ts
export async function record(
  orgId: OrgId,
  action: ActivityAction,
  input: ActivityRecordInput,
): Promise<ActivityEvent> {
  return activityRepo.insertActivity({
    orgId, action,
    actorId: input.actorId,
    subjectKind: input.subjectKind,
    subjectId: input.subjectId,
    projectId: input.projectId,
    summary: input.summary,
    metadata: input.metadata ?? {},
    occurredAt: toIsoTimestamp(new Date()),   // <-- stamped here, see item 6
```

`activityRepo.insertActivity` (`src/server/repositories/activity-repository.ts:14-37`) writes the row; note it always writes `metadata: "{}"` regardless of what was passed in (line 30), so the `metadata` bag on `ActivityRecordInput`/`record()` is effectively discarded before it reaches storage — only `summary` (a plain string) survives.

Fields on a row (`src/types/activity.ts:42-52`, `src/server/db/schema/activity.ts:4-34`): `id`, `orgId`, `action`, `actorId (nullable)`, `subjectKind`, `subjectId`, `projectId (nullable)`, `summary`, `metadata`, `occurredAt`.

**Entries are not written directly by the business logic.** Almost all of them come from `registerActivityListeners()` (`activity-service.ts:149-242`), which subscribes to the shared in-process event bus (`src/lib/event-bus.ts`) and turns each event into a `record()` call. - `issue.archived` — emitted at `issue-service.ts:208` (`archiveIssue`), never subscribed.
- `issue.restored` — not emitted anywhere (`ActivityAction` declares it, but there's no restore-issue event or service call at all; grep found no `issue.restored` emit site).
- `comment.deleted` — emitted at `src/server/services/comment-service.ts:138` (`deleteComment`), never subscribed.
- `comment.updated` — `updateComment` (`comment-service.ts:92-111`) never calls `emit()` at all; the type exists but nothing produces it.

### 2. Feed read / filter logic, especially project filtering

`listActivity()` — service (`activity-service.ts:68-75`) → repository (`activity-repository.ts:39-93`):

```ts
// activity-repository.ts:48-70

  orgPredicate(activityEvents.orgId, input.orgId),
  input.action === undefined || input.action.length === 0 ? undefined
    : inArray(activityEvents.action, [...input.action]),
  input.actorId === undefined ? undefined : eq(activityEvents.actorId, input.actorId),
  input.projectId === undefined ? undefined : eq(activityEvents.projectId, input.projectId),
  input.subjectKind === undefined ? undefined : eq(activityEvents.subjectKind, input.subjectKind),
  input.since === undefined ? undefined : gte(activityEvents.occurredAt, input.since),

  // [since, until) followed by [until, next).
```

- `src/app/(dashboard)/[orgSlug]/activity/page.tsx:61-65` — org-wide feed, only `orgId/limit/cursor`.

### 3. Export logic (CSV / JSON)

There are **two separate, inconsistent implementations**:

**a) `exportActivity()` service function** — `src/server/services/activity-service.ts:99-142`:

```ts
export async function exportActivity(actor: Actor, input: ExportActivityInput): Promise<string> {
  assertOrgScope(actor, input.orgId);
  assertCan(actor, "activity:export", activityResource(input.orgId));

  const org = await orgRepo.findOrgById(input.orgId);
  const flagEnabled = isEnabled("csv_export", { ... });

  if (input.format === "csv" && !flagEnabled) {
    throw new Error("CSV export is not included in this plan");
  }

  const page = await activityRepo.listActivity({
    orgId: input.orgId,
    since: input.since,
    until: input.until,
    limit: 100,          // <-- hardcoded, ignores any caller-supplied limit
    cursor: null,
  });

  if (input.format === "json") {
    return JSON.stringify(page.items, null, 2);
  }

  return toCsv(page.items.map((event) => ({...})), [...EXPORT_COLUMNS]);
}
```

- Range: `since`/`until` come from `exportActivitySchema` (`src/schemas/activity.ts`), both **required**, matching the repository's `gte(since)` / `lt(until)` — i.e. **inclusive lower bound, exclusive upper bound**.
- The `csv_export` plan-flag gate only applies to `format === "csv"`; **JSON export bypasses the flag check entirely** (only the `activity:export` permission check applies).
- `EXPORT_COLUMNS` (`activity-service.ts:36-43`) = `occurredAt, action, actorId, subjectKind, subjectId, summary` — **no `projectId` column**.
- Limit is hardcoded to **100** and not paginated — if a `since`/`until` window contains more than 100 events, the export silently returns only the most-recent 100 (rows are ordered `desc(occurredAt), desc(id)`), with no indication to the caller that entries were truncated.

**b) `/api/export/activity` route** — `src/app/api/export/activity/route.ts` — a second, independent implementation that also calls `listActivity` (via `EXPORT_PAGE_LIMIT = 100`, line 25), but:
- Gates **both** CSV and JSON behind `isEnabled("csv_export", ...)` (lines 51-53), run *before* `format` is even parsed — unlike `exportActivity()`, which only gates CSV.
- Its own `COLUMNS` (lines 27-34) **does include `projectId`**, unlike `EXPORT_COLUMNS` in `activity-service.ts`.
- Uses the same `exportActivitySchema` (required `since`/`until`), so same half-open range semantics.
- Returns `Response.json({ items: page.items, total: page.total })` for JSON (route.ts:79-81) vs. the service's `JSON.stringify(page.items, null, 2)` (no `total`) — different JSON shapes for the "same" export.

So the two export code paths disagree on: flag-gating of JSON, included columns, and JSON response shape, while sharing the same 100-row cap and inclusive/exclusive range.

### 5. "Assigned by" vs "assignee" naming

The event payload for `issue.assigned` (`src/types/event.ts:57-62`) correctly carries both:

```ts
"issue.assigned": EventEnvelope & {   // EventEnvelope.actorId = the person who did the assigning
  issueId: IssueId;
  projectId: ProjectId;
  previousAssigneeId: UserId | null;
  assigneeId: UserId;                 // the person being assigned
};
```

`issue-service.ts:180-186` emits it with the real actor in the envelope (`...actorEnvelope(actor)`, i.e. `actor.userId`) and the assignee separately as `assigneeId`.

But the activity-log listener discards the real actor and substitutes the assignee as the row's `actorId`:

```ts
// src/server/services/activity-service.ts:191-200
subscribe("issue.assigned", (payload) =>
  record(payload.orgId, "issue.assigned", {
    // The row is about the assignee: that is who the feed should name.
    actorId: payload.assigneeId,
    subjectKind: "issue",
    subjectId: payload.issueId,
    projectId: payload.projectId,
    summary: `Assigned to ${payload.assigneeId}`,
  }).then(() => undefined),
),
```

This means `payload.actorId` (who actually performed the assignment) is dropped entirely, and the stored `ActivityEvent.actorId` holds the assignee's id instead. Downstream, the feed UI resolves `actorId` to a name and renders it as the subject who performed the action:

```tsx
// src/components/domain/activity/activity-feed.tsx:71-84
const author = event.actorId === null ? undefined : actors[event.actorId];
...
<strong>{author?.name ?? "Taskflow"}</strong> {activityLabel(event.action)} — {event.summary}
```

So an "issue.assigned" row reads as `"<Assignee's name> assigned an issue — Assigned to <assigneeId>"`, effectively presenting the assignee as if they assigned themselves, and the person who actually performed the assignment (`payload.actorId`) never appears anywhere in the row.

---

### 6. Where the entry timestamp is set

`occurredAt` on the stored row is **always** stamped inside `record()` at write time, not taken from the triggering event's own timestamp:

```ts
// activity-service.ts:50-66
export async function record(...): Promise<ActivityEvent> {
  return activityRepo.insertActivity({
    ...
    occurredAt: toIsoTimestamp(new Date()),   // fresh Date() when record() runs
  });
}
```

Every `TaskflowEventMap` event already carries its own `occurredAt` via `EventEnvelope` (`src/types/event.ts:16-20`), stamped when the event is created — `envelope()`/`actorEnvelope()` in `src/server/services/_support.ts:111-118`:

```ts
export function envelope(orgId: OrgId, actorId: UserId | null): EventEnvelope {
  return { orgId, actorId, occurredAt: toIsoTimestamp(new Date()) };
}
```

`record()` never reads `payload.occurredAt` — it re-stamps with `new Date()` inside the event-bus handler. Normally the gap is negligible since `emit()` awaits all handlers synchronously (`src/lib/event-bus.ts:54-72`), but `comment-service.ts` shows the payload's `occurredAt` is sometimes deliberately overridden to reflect the true domain moment:

```ts
// comment-service.ts:132-143 (deleteComment)
const { archivedAt } = archivePatch();
const archived = await commentRepo.archiveComment(input.orgId, input.commentId);

await emit("comment.deleted", {
  ...actorEnvelope(actor),
  occurredAt: archivedAt,   // explicit override of the envelope's occurredAt
  commentId: archived.id,
  issueId: archived.issueId,
});
```

Even where a producer sets a specific `occurredAt` like this, `record()`'s handler ignores it and substitutes the time the listener happened to run — so the audit log's timestamp is "written time," not the domain "created/occurred time" the event itself may carry. (In this specific `comment.deleted` case it's moot anyway, since that event isn't subscribed by `registerActivityListeners` at all — see item 4.)

The one exception is `organization.updated`, written via the direct `record()` call in `organization-service.ts:68`, which has no separate "event occurred" timestamp to diverge from — write time and occurrence time are the same call.</result>

```ts

  assertOrgScope(actor, input.orgId);
  assertCan(actor, "activity:export", activityResource(input.orgId));

  const org = await orgRepo.findOrgById(input.orgId);

  if (input.format === "csv" && !flagEnabled) {

  const page = await activityRepo.listActivity({
    orgId: input.orgId,
    since: input.since,
    until: input.until,
    limit: 100,          // <-- hardcoded, ignores any caller-supplied limit
    cursor: null,

  if (input.format === "json") {
    return JSON.stringify(page.items, null, 2);

  return toCsv(page.items.map((event) => ({...})), [...EXPORT_COLUMNS]);
```

- The `csv_export` plan-flag gate only applies to `format === "csv"`; **JSON export bypasses the flag check entirely** (only the `activity:export` permission check applies).
- `EXPORT_COLUMNS` (`activity-service.ts:36-43`) = `occurredAt, action, actorId, subjectKind, subjectId, summary` — **no `projectId` column**.
- Limit is hardcoded to **100** and not paginated — if a `since`/`until` window contains more than 100 events, the export silently returns only the most-recent 100 (rows are ordered `desc(occurredAt), desc(id)`), with no indication to the caller that entries were truncated.

**b) `/api/export/activity` route** — `src/app/api/export/activity/route.ts` — a second, independent implementation that also calls `listActivity` (via `EXPORT_PAGE_LIMIT = 100`, line 25), but:

### 5. "Assigned by" vs "assignee" naming

The event payload for `issue.assigned` (`src/types/event.ts:57-62`) correctly carries both:

```ts
"issue.assigned": EventEnvelope & {   // EventEnvelope.actorId = the person who did the assigning
  issueId: IssueId;
  projectId: ProjectId;
  previousAssigneeId: UserId | null;
  assigneeId: UserId;                 // the person being assigned
};
```

`issue-service.ts:180-186` emits it with the real actor in the envelope (`...actorEnvelope(actor)`, i.e. `actor.userId`) and the assignee separately as `assigneeId`.

But the activity-log listener discards the real actor and substitutes the assignee as the row's `actorId`:

```ts
// src/server/services/activity-service.ts:191-200
subscribe("issue.assigned", (payload) =>
  record(payload.orgId, "issue.assigned", {
    // The row is about the assignee: that is who the feed should name.
    actorId: payload.assigneeId,
    subjectKind: "issue",
    subjectId: payload.issueId,
    projectId: payload.projectId,
    summary: `Assigned to ${payload.assigneeId}`,
  }).then(() => undefined),
),
```

This means `payload.actorId` (who actually performed the assignment) is dropped entirely, and the stored `ActivityEvent.actorId` holds the assignee's id instead. Downstream, the feed UI resolves `actorId` to a name and renders it as the subject who performed the action:

```tsx
// src/components/domain/activity/activity-feed.tsx:71-84
const author = event.actorId === null ? undefined : actors[event.actorId];
...
<strong>{author?.name ?? "Taskflow"}</strong> {activityLabel(event.action)} — {event.summary}
```

So an "issue.assigned" row reads as `"<Assignee's name> assigned an issue — Assigned to <assigneeId>"`, effectively presenting the assignee as if they assigned themselves, and the person who actually performed the assignment (`payload.actorId`) never appears anywhere in the row.

### 6. Where the entry timestamp is set

`occurredAt` on the stored row is **always** stamped inside `record()` at write time, not taken from the triggering event's own timestamp:

```ts
// activity-service.ts:50-66
export async function record(...): Promise<ActivityEvent> {
  return activityRepo.insertActivity({
    ...
    occurredAt: toIsoTimestamp(new Date()),   // fresh Date() when record() runs
  });
}
```

Every `TaskflowEventMap` event already carries its own `occurredAt` via `EventEnvelope` (`src/types/event.ts:16-20`), stamped when the event is created — `envelope()`/`actorEnvelope()` in `src/server/services/_support.ts:111-118`:

```ts
export function envelope(orgId: OrgId, actorId: UserId | null): EventEnvelope {
  return { orgId, actorId, occurredAt: toIsoTimestamp(new Date()) };
}
```

`record()` never reads `payload.occurredAt` — it re-stamps with `new Date()` inside the event-bus handler. Normally the gap is negligible since `emit()` awaits all handlers synchronously (`src/lib/event-bus.ts:54-72`), but `comment-service.ts` shows the payload's `occurredAt` is sometimes deliberately overridden to reflect the true domain moment:

```ts
// comment-service.ts:132-143 (deleteComment)
const { archivedAt } = archivePatch();
const archived = await commentRepo.archiveComment(input.orgId, input.commentId);

await emit("comment.deleted", {
  ...actorEnvelope(actor),
  occurredAt: archivedAt,   // explicit override of the envelope's occurredAt
  commentId: archived.id,
  issueId: archived.issueId,
});
```

Even where a producer sets a specific `occurredAt` like this, `record()`'s handler ignores it and substitutes the time the listener happened to run — so the audit log's timestamp is "written time," not the domain "created/occurred time" the event itself may carry.   isoTimestampSchema,
  orgIdSchema,
  pageRequestSchema,
  projectIdSchema,
  userIdSchema,
} from "./common";

  "organization.updated",
  "project.created",
  "project.updated",
  "project.archived",
  "project.restored",
  "issue.created",
  "issue.updated",
  "issue.status_changed",
  "issue.assigned",
  "issue.archived",
  "issue.restored",
  "comment.created",
  "comment.updated",
  "comment.deleted",
  "member.invited",
  "member.joined",
  "member.role_changed",
  "member.removed",
  "billing.plan_changed",
  "flag.toggled",
]);

export const activitySubjectKindSchema = z.enum([
  "organization",
  "project",
  "issue",
  "comment",
  "member",
  "subscription",
  "feature_flag",
]);

export const activityFilterSchema = z
  .object({
    orgId: orgIdSchema,
    action: z.array(activityActionSchema).optional(),
    actorId: userIdSchema.optional(),
    projectId: projectIdSchema.optional(),
    subjectKind: activitySubjectKindSchema.optional(),
    since: isoTimestampSchema.optional(),

  orgId: orgIdSchema,
  since: isoTimestampSchema,
  until: isoTimestampSchema,
  format: z.enum(["csv", "json"]).default("csv"),
});

export type ActivityFilterInput = z.infer<typeof activityFilterSchema>;
export type ExportActivityInput = z.infer<typeof exportActivitySchema>;

## 2. `src/lib/csv.ts` — `toCsv`

```ts
export function toCsv(
  rows: readonly Readonly<Record<string, string | number | boolean | null>>[],
  columns: readonly string[],
): string {
  const lines: string[] = [columns.map(escapeCsvValue).join(",")];
  for (const row of rows) {
    lines.push(
      columns.map((column) => escapeCsvValue(row[column] ?? null)).join(","),
    );
  }
  return lines.join("\r\n");
}
```

`escapeCsvValue` (line 12-17) is typed `value: string | number | boolean | null` and does `String(value)`. **`toCsv` only handles primitives** (string/number/boolean/null) at the type level and via `String()` at runtime — there is no special handling for objects or arrays. If an object/array were passed (e.g. an unstringified `metadata` field), `String(value)` would stringify it as `"[object Object]"` or `Array.prototype.toString()` output (comma-joined, no proper JSON/quoting), not valid CSV-safe JSON. Both current callers (`activity-service.ts` and `route.ts`'s `toRow`) build rows manually with only primitive fields, so `metadata` is currently excluded from CSV export rows.

25	export type ActivityRecordInput = {

28	  subjectId: string;

42	  "projectId",

44	] as const;

49	/**
50	 * Appends one audit row. Deliberately takes no `Actor`: the writer is usually
51	 * an event handler running outside a request, and the row's `actorId` comes
52	 * from the event payload rather than from an authenticated principal. The
53	 * timestamp is likewise supplied by the caller — it is the moment the action
54	 * happened, not the moment this function runs, so a background job that
55	 * writes the row late still files it under the right time.
56	 */
57	export async function record(
58	  orgId: OrgId,
59	  action: ActivityAction,
60	  input: ActivityRecordInput,
61	): Promise<ActivityEvent> {
62	  return activityRepo.insertActivity({
63	    orgId,
64	    action,
65	    actorId: input.actorId,
66	    subjectKind: input.subjectKind,
67	    subjectId: input.subjectId,
68	    projectId: input.projectId,
69	    summary: input.summary,
70	    metadata: input.metadata ?? {},
71	    occurredAt: input.occurredAt,
72	  });
73	}

75	export async function listActivity(

77	  input: ActivityFilterInput,
78	): Promise<Page<ActivityEvent>> {
79	  assertOrgScope(actor, input.orgId);
80	  assertCan(actor, "activity:read", activityResource(input.orgId));
81	  return activityRepo.listActivity(input);
82	}

84	/** Groups a feed page by calendar day, newest day first. */
85	export function groupByDay(
86	  events: readonly ActivityEvent[],
87	): readonly ActivityGroup[] {
88	  const byDay = new Map<string, ActivityEvent[]>();
89	
90	  for (const event of events) {
91	    const day = event.occurredAt.slice(0, 10);
92	    const bucket = byDay.get(day) ?? [];
93	    bucket.push(event);
94	    byDay.set(day, bucket);
95	  }
96	
97	  return [...byDay.entries()]
98	    .sort(([a], [b]) => (a < b ? 1 : -1))
99	    .map(([day, dayEvents]) => ({ day, events: dayEvents }));
100	}

102	/**
103	 * CSV (or JSON) export of the audit log. Gated twice: on `activity:export`
104	 * for the role, and on the `csv_export` flag for the plan.
105	 */
106	export async function exportActivity(
107	  actor: Actor,
108	  input: ExportActivityInput,
109	): Promise<string> {
110	  assertOrgScope(actor, input.orgId);
111	  assertCan(actor, "activity:export", activityResource(input.orgId));
112	
113	  const org = await orgRepo.findOrgById(input.orgId);
114	  const flagEnabled = isEnabled("csv_export", {
115	    orgId: input.orgId,
116	    userId: actor.userId,
117	    plan: org?.plan ?? "free",
118	    role: actor.role,
119	    overrides: org?.settings.enabledFlagOverrides,
120	  });
121	
122	  if (input.format === "csv" && !flagEnabled) {
123	    throw new Error("CSV export is not included in this plan");
124	  }
125	
126	  const items = await drainActivityRange(input.orgId, input.since, input.until);
127	
128	  if (input.format === "json") {
129	    return JSON.stringify(items, null, 2);
130	  }
131	
132	  return toCsv(
133	    items.map((event) => ({
134	      occurredAt: event.occurredAt,
135	      action: event.action,
136	      actorId: event.actorId,
137	      subjectKind: event.subjectKind,
138	      subjectId: event.subjectId,
139	      projectId: event.projectId,
140	      summary: event.summary,
141	    })),
142	    [...EXPORT_COLUMNS],
143	  );
144	}

146	/**
147	 * Pages through every entry in `[since, until]`, newest first, with no cap —
148	 * an export must contain the whole range however many rows it holds.
149	 */
150	async function drainActivityRange(
151	  orgId: OrgId,
152	  since: IsoTimestamp,
153	  until: IsoTimestamp,
154	): Promise<readonly ActivityEvent[]> {
155	  const items: ActivityEvent[] = [];
156	  let cursor: string | null = null;
157	
158	  for (;;) {
159	    const page = await activityRepo.listActivity({
160	      orgId,
161	      since,
162	      until,
163	      limit: EXPORT_PAGE_SIZE,
164	      cursor,
165	    });
166	
167	    items.push(...page.items);
168	    if (page.nextCursor === null) break;
169	    cursor = page.nextCursor;
170	  }
171	
172	  return items;
173	}

  - `record()` now takes the actual `occurredAt` from the caller instead of stamping `new Date()`, so late-written entries keep the real action time.
  - Added listeners for every previously-missing action: `project.updated`, `project.restored`, `issue.updated`, `issue.archived`, `comment.updated`, `comment.deleted`, `member.joined`, `member.removed`, `flag.toggled`.
  - Fixed `issue.assigned` to record the real actor (`payload.actorId`) instead of the assignee.
  - `issue.status_changed` and `comment.*` now carry `projectId` so project filtering surfaces them.
  - `exportActivity` now drains the full range via cursor pagination instead of capping at 100.
- **`src/server/repositories/activity-repository.ts`**: range filter is now inclusive on both ends (`lte` instead of `lt` for `until`); `metadata` is now actually persisted (`JSON.stringify(event.metadata)`) instead of being hardcoded to `"{}"`.

- **`src/app/api/export/activity/route.ts`**: also drains the full range instead of capping at 100 entries.
